0473_Report_from_Rhode_Island_01_18_08_1.sy: The film "Report from Rhode Island" highlights the history and community spirit of Rhode Island, focusing on its founding by Roger Williams, who advocated for religious freedom. It showcases Providence as a bustling city with a strong industrial base, particularly in wartime production. The film also contrasts the historical opulence of Newport with its current state, emphasizing community engagement and local governance. It depicts the resilience of Rhode Island's residents during World War II, including youth programs and military training efforts that contribute to the war effort. Keywords Rhode Island, Roger Williams, Providence, religious freedom, industrial base, WWII, Newport, community spirit, local governance, youth programs, military training

49274OurChangingWorldPearlOfTheOrient.sy: Released in 1948 by Paul White and directed by William Winter, "Pearl of the Orient" tells the story of the Philippines as it rose from the disaster of WWII to become a modern nation. The film is notable as it contains native music and songs recorded in the field, along with footage of Filipino arts and crafts including weaving. At 1:12, modern Manila is shown, still bearing many scars of war but appearing bustling and full of life. Starting at 1:30, rural life in the mountains of Luzon is shown along with indigenous handicrafts and at 2:04, native ceremonies including the warrior dance. These are members of the Igorot tribe who live in the mountains of northern Luzon, the largest island of the Philippines. The name Igorot means "mountaineer" in the Tagalog language. There are about 10 main ethnic groups among the Igorot, each with its own culture. At 2:26 Igorot marriage ceremonies are seen. The film also shows rice farming at 3:00 using flood irrigation methods, the harvest with water buffalo providing some motive power, and a harvest dance called a "rice ballet" by the narrator at 5:00. Fish and then pork is seen being cooked at 5:50, a diet that continues into the 21st Century. At 6:45, a cock fight is shown with the roosters having long, sharp metal shivs attached to their legs. At 7:19 the Sulu Islands are shown and the Moro people. The Moro people is a coined term for the population of Muslims in the Philippines, forming the largest non-Catholic group in the country,…

CHAN-915.sy: MPEG This animation shows how sound waves are generated in the Perseus cluster from its central supermassive black hole. The gas that fills the cluster of galaxies is shown in red. The animation then zooms in to show the cluster's central black hole, which is seen as a white point. Next, blue-white jets of high-energy particles and magnetic fields blow out from the black hole, forming dark cavities in the cluster gas. When these cavities slow down, sound waves break off and travel away from the cavities. The animation then dissolves into Chandra's X-ray image of the cluster.

SVS-3420.sy: The SeaWiFS instrument aboard the Seastar satellite has been collecting ocean data since 1997. By monitoring the color of reflected light via satellite, scientists can determine how successfully plant life is photosynthesizing. A measurement of photosynthesis is essentially a measurement of successful growth, and growth means successful use of ambient carbon. This animation represents nearly a decade's worth of data taken by the SeaWiFS instrument, showing the abundance of life in the sea. Dark blue represents warmer areas where there is little life due to lack of nutrients, and greens and reds represent cooler nutrient-rich areas. The nutrient-rich areas include coastal regions where cold water rises from the sea floor bringing nutrients along and areas at the mouths of rivers where the rivers have brought nutrients into the ocean from the land. Note: Animation of a rotating globe showing nearly a decade's worth of SeaWiFS data from 1997 to 2006. Data Collected: 08/29/1997 - 10/23/2006. Animator: Alex Kekesi (GST). Scientist: Gene Feldman (NASA/GSFC). Platforms/Sensors/Data Sets: SeaStar/SeaWiFS, SeaStar/SeaWiFS/Sea Surface Temperature.

TwinPeaksTunnel1917.sy: Shot in the years after the great earthquake and fire which leveled The City, Twin Peaks Tunnel was intended to promote the development of Western portions of San Francisco. Twin Peaks Tunnel was shot by the Pathescope film company for a local real estate firm. It documents construction of what was then claimed to be the longest municipal tunnel in the world. The film includes footage of the construction of the tunnel and the clearing of Sutro Forest, as well as development of the West Portal, St. Francis Wood, and Westwood Park neighborhoods. City officials, engineers, workers and ordinary citizens are also seen in the film. According to historian David Kiehn, the film was produced for the Baldwin and Howell Real Estate Company, located on Kearny Street in San Francisco. Newspaper advertisements also indicate that the film was first shown on October 13, 1917 - most likely in a San Francisco storefront. Funds to restore and preserve Twin Peaks Tunnel were provided through a grant from the National Film Preservation Foundation. The original 28mm copy of Twin Peaks Tunnel is in the collection of the Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum. The museum also holds the 35mm preservation negative and two 35mm positive prints.

What_Price_Vengeance_1937.sy: The film was part of the British Quota Law that existed in the 1930's that basically said in order for films produced in the U.S. by U.S. producers and companies to be shown in Great Britain or any of the colonies, a certain number of films shot somewhere in the British Empire, with the majority of the cast and crew British subjects, had to be shown in the U.S.A. This posed no problems for the major studios who either had production facilities in England or working agreements with the major British producers, but Columbia had neither. In order to comply with the British Quota, so Columbia films could be shown in England and its far-flung outposts, Columbia entered into an agreement with Commonwealth Studios, headed by Canadian-producer Kenneth J. Bishop, in Willows Park, Victoria, British Columbia, Canada to finance and shoot films there for distribution through Columbia's film exchanges. Most of these films starred imported Columbia contractees such as Rita Hayworth, Charles Quigley, Rosalind Keith, Charles Starrett and others, but the vast majority of cast and crew was made up of subjects of the Crown. As such, there were a couple of dozen B-features or westerns shot in Canada with the cast filled with names such as Finis Barton, Robert Rideout, Arthur Kerr, Reginald Hincks, Edgar Edwards et al, directed or written by people such as Del Lord (Canadian-born), J. rpnewsoftoday001.sy: The film is a montage of various news events and everyday scenes from the 1940s, showcasing both military and civilian life. It begins with young pilots training at Kelly Field in Texas, emphasizing the growing military preparedness of America. The scenes shift to the intense production efforts in munitions factories, with skilled workers crafting weaponry to support the nation's defense. The film also highlights the unwavering dedication of political leaders like President Roosevelt and British figures such as King George and Winston Churchill during the turbulent times of World War II. Interspersed with wartime footage are lighter segments showcasing American culture, such as parades, sports events, and everyday life. There are glimpses of soldiers and civilians, bustling city streets, neighborhood activities, and leisure moments like couples walking through gardens or families enjoying picnics. The narrative also touches on the opium trade, with detailed scenes of its production, usage, and law enforcement efforts to combat it. The film further includes a variety of community and sports activities, featuring parades, baseball games, and football matches, symbolizing national pride and unity. It culminates with an emphasis on community spirit and teamwork, highlighting a nationwide campaign by Standard Oil to promote service and unity among its dealers, using sports metaphors to underscore the importance of collaboration and collective effort in achieving success.

series:an-age-of-kings-1960.sy: Groundbreaking 15-part BBC drama serial created by Peter Dews, written by Eric Crozier, and directed by Michael Hayes, adapting the eight William Shakespeare history plays which comprise the two Henriad s. These cover events in England and France during the second half of the Hundred Years' War, and the subsequent Wars of the Roses. They are: * Richard II (2 episodes) * Henry IV, Part 1 (2 episodes) * Henry IV, Part 2 (2 episodes) * Henry V (2 episodes) * Henry VI, Part 1 (1 episode) * Henry VI, Part 2 (2 episodes) * Henry VI, Part 3 (2 episodes) * Richard III (2 episodes) Stars David William as Richard II, Tom Fleming as Henry IV, Robert Hardy as Henry V, Terry Scully as Henry VI, and Paul Daneman as Richard III, as well as a whole host of other great British actors, including Julian Glover, Geoffrey Bayldon, Eileen Atkins, Michael Graham Cox, William Squire, Judi Dench, and some then-unknown Scottish guy named Sean Connery; wonder if he ever did anything else.

silent-panoramic-view-of-the-golden-gate.sy: This picture was taken from the front end of a train during a trip from the famous Cliff House to Bakers Beach along the shore of the Golden Gate. The train runs along the brink of the cliff and gives a perfect representation of the objects that meet the eye prior to entering the Golden Gate. One of the features of this picture is the stirring ride along the very edge of the cliff, the track being laid in places within a foot of the brink, and far below can be seen the huge breakers dashing against the foot of the cliff. (Edison Catalog)

the-prodigal-son_202411.sy: The Prodigal Son is a 1923 British silent historical film directed by A. E. Coleby and starring Stewart Rome, Henry Victor and Edith Bishop. The film is an adaptation of Hall Caine's 1904 novel The Prodigal Son, set in Iceland and the French Riviera. It was noted as a long film, reported variously at three or over four hours. The film's original release length as 18,454 feet made it the longest commercially made British film. It was shown in two consecutive parts, the second part being entitled The Return of the Prodigal.

way-for-a-sailor_1930.sy: Jack is a sailor who lives to go to sea. A typical sailor, he is always broke and has been in seven jails in the last seven ports. The one girl he tries to impress the most is in London and his mates call her 'the Eskimo'. For two years, he approaches her every time he docks near London, and for two years, Joan rejects the expensive gifts he brings to her and ignores any and all advances he makes. She wants nothing to do with a sailor. When Jack uses trickery to convince Joan to marry him, Joan leaves him when she finds out the truth about his so called new life. There are rough seas ahead as Jack tries to get Joan to come back to him.

xd-11164-womens-liberation-vwr-1.sy: A 1970 news segment about the various factions and interests of the Women’s Liberation Movement produced and hosted by ABC News correspondent Marlene Sanders. Sanders, as a female journalist breaking into the industry in 1960s, was the first female television correspondent in Vietnam, the first female anchor on a U.S. network television evening newscast, and the first female vice president of ABC News. “Women’s Liberation” was the first of her seven documentaries on the topic. A woman speaks to an audience how “boys are raised to be something” while girls are “raised to be housewives” (0:52). ABC News correspondent Marlene Sanders discusses the Women’s Liberation Movement questioning the role of women in society (1:16). Introduces the rising movement at University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill as they issue demands to the university. The students perform skits demonstrating the inequalities faced by women (1:50). Linda Fisher, a member of the movement at UNC, discusses what men can gain from the movement (5:10). A self-defense class in action and an attendee is interviewed about what the class means for women (6:15). A pro-choice march with attendees holding up banners of their demands (7:21). Attorney Nancy Sterns speaks to a marching crowd about the movement and the gains they have made so far (8:27). Folk singer Mary Sanders Shartle sings to the crowd (9:39).
